utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Turning now to Sirokaca. It is the Prosecution's case that the city of Sarajevo was heavily shelled, damaging and destroying civilian targets, causing the deaths of several civilians and injuring others from on or about 28 May 1992, which forms Schedule G(1) of the indictment. The Prosecution cite supporting evidence from three witnesses who address the shelling of different parts of Sarajevo, including the neighbourhood of Sirokaca. This is annex B, Roman lower case numeral xx, with the contention that Serbian forces were responsible. The evidence presented by the Prosecution to this extent is not capable of supporting a conviction, as it fails to prove that the Serbian military strategy was responsible for and had the intention to spread terror amongst the civilian population. It is for the Prosecution to prove: (A) by which side this military action has been authorised against unlawful targets; (B) that within those illegitimate actions there was the intent to target the civilian population in order to terrorise; (C) that the intent to kill civilians existed; (D) that the intent to inflict injuries other than murder existed. Your Honours, that is the requirements as set forth in the Galic case on the motion for judgement of acquittal under Rule 98 bis on behalf of the defendant General Stanislav Galic, 2 September 2002, section 7. In the Prosecution pre-trial brief in public annex B, page lower case Roman numeral xx, the Prosecution has down that there are three witness testimonies which support General Mladic's guilt in relation to Schedule G(1) of the indictment. These witnesses are RM115, RM120, and RM168. Both RM115 and RM120 are protected witnesses that gave evidence before the Chamber on 27 August 2012 and 29 through 30 January 2013 respectively. However, the sole eye-witness to support the Prosecution's case in relation to Sirokaca is the remaining witness, Fadila Tarcin. While the other two witnesses testify about other areas in Sarajevo, this witness gave evidence about the incident in Sirokaca on 28/29 May 1992 via a 92 ter statement and addendum and oral testimony on 2 October 2012. The Prosecution has not called any other survivors who could provide an eye-witness account of the events, any military insiders who could attest to the military strategy and intent of the armies, nor any expert or expert reports that support the Prosecution's contention that the Serb forces were responsible for the attacks in Sirokaca specifically. Recourse to Tarcin's evidence demonstrates that there is a total collapse of the Prosecutor's case and therefore that an acquittal should be entered. The witness's 92 ter evidence does not explicitly attribute the shelling to any particular force. Her written evidence notes a subsequently broadcasted intercepted conversation allegedly featuring General Mladic, but states that she "never linked it to what happened to her," which is page 3, paragraph 12, of her witness statement, which is Exhibit P00281. In the Rule 92 ter addendum, P00282, she states at page 2, paragraph 3, that she heard from locals that the shell that wounded her was fired from Borije, due east of Sirokaca, and that she was able to see where the shell had impacted on her neighbour's house. When subject to cross-examination, Tarcin explained that the impact of the shell on her neighbour's house "was facing downhill, that is to say facing town." That's transcript page 3347 [sic], lines 20 through 21. When asked by the Chamber if this meant that the impact was from the direction of the river, from the valley, rather than from uphill, the witness answered in the affirmative at 33 -- transcript page 3347, lines 22 through 25. This evidence stands in direct contradiction to the Prosecution's case that the Serbian forces were responsible for the shelling, as she indicated the directionality of the shelling to have come from within the city, thus indirectly attributing it to the Muslim forces. On this basis, the Prosecution's case in relation to Sirokaca has collapsed, as there is simply no evidence that supports their case and is capable of sustaining a conviction against General Mladic for causing and authorising this shelling that injured Witness Tarcin. With regards to intent, if on the basis of Tarcin's evidence the Prosecutor is unable to prove that Serb forces were responsible for the shelling of Sirokaca, then it cannot show that military action to the end was authorised by the Serbs with the intention of targeting the civilian population. Thus, on the basis of Tarcin's evidence, the Prosecution's case has collapsed in relation to the shelling of Sirokaca and judgement of acquittal should be entered. Your Honours, I will now address the Defence's submission challenging the veracity of the Prosecution's individual charges as to religious sites under the ambit of Rule 98 bis. Under Counts 7 and 8 of the indictment, the Prosecution alleges that destruction of cultural monuments and religious sites is a part of their case against General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, in order to avoid any confusion, you were quoting transcript page 3347, unless that's a mistake, the downhill passage, which according to my system should be 3447, so as to avoid anyone later not finding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your records are much more reliable than mine as I stand here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have the same records on our computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Schedule D of the indictment contains the various municipalities and site locations which are alleged to comprise the Prosecutor's allegations as to destruction of religious sites. We respectfully assert that the Prosecution's case presented at trial has been deficient and has failed to meet even the reduced burden of proof to survive the Rule 98 bis stage. For this reason, the Defence invites the Chamber to throw out this segment of the Prosecution's case at this stage, because its case has completely broken down to the extent that the Prosecution is left without a case. To maintain the charges would be to force the Defence to dedicate precious resources to counter charges that are indefensible on the basis of the evidence proffered. Once again, the Defence reiterates that the purpose of the Rule 98 bis proceedings is to strike out allegations that the Prosecution has failed to adduce any evidence capable of supporting a conviction to ensure due process and expeditiousness and urges Your Honours to keep this at the forefront of your thoughts during the next submission. Of specific relevance to the objections raised by the Defence is the Appeals Chamber judgement in Hadzihasanovic and Kubura at paragraph 51. It was held that the accused's right to a fair trial may be infringed if he is erroneously required to answer the Prosecution's case. I urge Your Honours to take into account that if the goal of these proceedings has been the ascertainment of the truth, the evidence adduced by the Prosecution must be assessed as to the truth it has revealed, and if it is wholly inconsistent with the allegations of guilt in the indictment and the Prosecution pre-trial brief, the relevant charges against General Mladic must be stricken and dismissed at this stage. As such we submit it would be an infringement of General Mladic's fair trial rights if forced to expend resources to defend against the allegations relating to destruction of cultural monuments and sacred sites. I note from the outset that there has been no proof that General Mladic ordered or is criminally liable for the crimes of others as to destruction of sacred and religious sites under any mode of liability. There are a total of 11 municipalities that remain a part of this case. I will focus on the three most glaring examples of how the Prosecution's case has failed to support these allegations. I will address Bijeljina, Kalinovik, and Pale municipalities. Schedule D(1) relates to three locations in Bijeljina municipality, consisting of three mosques. The Prosecution pre-trial brief at annex B, Schedule D, page lowercase Roman xi specifies that for these three mosques the Prosecution's best case cannot even identify any known perpetrators for their destruction. The pre-trial brief identifies two witnesses, RM618 and RM513, and two documents, 65 ter number 03431 and 65 ter number 13410, that are meant to support and prove the allegations as to these three sacred sites in Bijeljina. Your Honours, neither of these two documents have been admitted into evidence and thus cannot be relied upon to support this allegation at this stage. RM618, that is the expert report of Andras Riedlmayer. During his in-court examination, Mr. Riedlmayer did not offer any testimony as to these three mosques in Bijeljina. P2513 is the expert report produced by Mr. Riedlmayer. There is an annex to the report which purports to give information about perpetrators of the destruction of sacred sites. There are four entries for Bijeljina, none of them are identified as the three sites that are set forth in the indictment. Incidentally, for the four sites that are referenced, the sole source relied upon by Mr. Riedlmayer is informants' statements and news reports, although only one informant is identified for each. P2503, another expert report of Professor Riedlmayer, likewise has no mention of these three locations in Bijeljina. P2511 is the database offered by Mr. Riedlmayer into evidence. At record number 13 of the same, the Atmacici mosque in Bijeljina, there is no information on the alleged perpetrators of the destruction, nor any particulars as to the date or the manner of the damage being inflicted. The sole source is anonymous hearsay information in the medzlis of the Islamic community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the Atmacici mosque one of the three?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. To be clear, the three that are listed in the indictment are Atmacici, Janjari and Srednja Trnova. As to the Janjari mosque, this is record 14 of P2511, and again it gives no information as to alleged perpetrators, the manner, and the date of the damage. Indeed, there are two equally anonymous hearsay sources relied on by Riedlmayer, one which states that the mosque was destroyed, whereas the other states that the mosque was in an unfinished state of construction when the war began and was never finished. As to the third location in the indictment for Bijeljina, Srednja Trnova mosque, this is record 15 of P2511, and again there is not sufficient information as to perpetrators or the manner of destruction. In fact, the information is that residents say it was intact when they left and found destroyed when they returned. Again, the source of the information is unknown hearsay declarants as reported by another hearsay source. In each of these cases, the evidence at best provides not a single eye-witness account that could identify the perpetrators or manner of destruction to prove the allegations in the indictment. The other records pertaining to Bijeljina in Riedlmayer's report cannot be relied upon or reviewed by the Chamber, as they are not specified in either the indictment or the pre-trial brief. RM513 is a protected witness who testified about a wholly different subject, and in their in-court testimony made no reference of these sacred sites or of what happened to them. P1054 under seal is the statement of this individual. Following the guidance of your Chamber and I think it's important for the public to hear, I will talk about what is in the statement without revealing the identity of this witness, so that the public can see what type of evidence is being presented by the Prosecution on this score. Paragraph 77 of this statement makes no specific mention of these particular religious sites set forth in the indictment, but rather states that unnamed sites were destroyed and as to the source says: "This information was spoken about in Bijeljina." Rumour and unknown hearsay, Your Honours, that is the best case this Prosecution has been able to offer as to these three sites from Schedule D(1), bolstered by unsubstantiated accounts of other sites that are not even in the indictment. Is it fair to force an accused to answer such allegations? In the Mrksic Rule 98 bis decision at transcript page 11311 through 11312, the Court, relying on the Jelisic Appeals Chamber, stated in essence that the Chamber is required at this stage to assume that the Prosecution's evidence is, and I quote, "entitled to credence unless incapable of belief." "In essence, a Rule 98 bis motion will succeed if there is no evidence supporting a particular count or if the only relevant evidence is so incapable of belief that it could not properly sustain a conviction, even when the evidence is taken at its highest for the Prosecution." Your Honours, I submit the foregoing can be regarded as either not being any evidence or evidence that is incapable of belief. Just the other week the ICC had a judgement issued by the Appeals Chamber in the Bosco Ntaganda case, and I would like to discuss with you the dissenting opinion of Judge Christine Van den Wyngaert, who Your Honours know as she was a former colleague of the Bench of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT STATED
utterances.text: "I am also of the opinion that Pre-Trial Chamber II (hereinafter: 'Pre-Trial Chamber') erred in its sole reliance on anonymous hearsay evidence contained in press releases, blog articles, and two UN group of expert reports. Such evidence must be treated with utmost caution in the context of a criminal trial and without considerably more independently verified information cannot, in my view, be safely relied upon to justify the continued detention of Mr. Bosco Ntaganda."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT CONTINUES
utterances.text: "The Internal Criminal Court (hereinafter: 'ICC') and ad hoc tribunals have traditionally employed a flexible approach to the admissibility of evidence, ostensibly a civil law influence within a broadly adversarial system. Rather than systematically rejecting the admissibility of any particular category of evidence, Judges have been afforded broad discretion to balance probative value with prejudicial effect. However, the fact that certain types of evidence, such as anonymous hearsay, are not automatically excluded from the proceedings does not mean that they are therefore safe to rely on. Whether they are or not can only be determined on a case-by-case basis, which, in the case of anonymous hearsay is a difficult task, considering the sources of the information are unknown ... at the ICC too, Pre-Trial and Trial Judges are more and more relegating anonymous hearsay evidence to something which can, at best, potentially corroborate other evidence, rather than as stand-alone source of information that possesses significant probative value per se."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT CONCLUDES
utterances.text: "What I think warrants emphasis, however, is that this more cautious approach to anonymous hearsay evidence is not something that derives from the whim of a number of Judges. Instead, it brings us closer to the standard that always should have been applied when assessing such evidence. Indeed, I'm not aware of any other system of criminal justice, be it national or international, where anonymous hearsay is given any serious probative value, if it is considered/admitted at all. I can think of no good reason why this Court should take a different approach, let alone what could justify basing judicial decisions pertaining to the freedom of individuals on evidence that is inherently fragile and against which the suspect has no meaningful opportunity to defend him or herself." Your Honours, we respectfully submit that the logic behind Judge Van den Wyngaert's words applies equally here to the ICTY, and especially at this stage, and to allegations in the indictment that are not supported by any other evidence save for anonymous or unknown hearsay. I would now direct Your Honours to Kalinovik. The indictment identifies at Schedule D(6) four mosques in Kalinovik for which the criminal responsibility of General Mladic is asserted. The Prosecution pre-trial brief again is unable to identify any alleged perpetrators, let alone any persons that General Mladic would be responsible for. As to Kalinovik, no documents were identified as supporting this allegation and there are three witnesses: Mr. Riedlmayer, RM035, and RM034. Again, Professor Riedlmayer in court offered no evidence as to these four locations in Kalinovik. P2513, his expert report, as to Kalinovik only has an entry for the Ulog mosque and not the other three. As to the Ulog mosque, it is not specific as to who blew up the mosque, when, or for what purpose, except to say it was done by Serbs and is based according to the information from the Centre for Islamic Studies, again unknown, anonymous hearsay. Looking to P2511, entry 168 is the Ulog mosque and this offers no support for who destroyed it. Entry 169 is the Hotovlje mosque in Kalinovik, and again there is no information contained as to the perpetrators or the manner of destruction that suggests criminal liability. The only sources listed for the scant information are the Muslim community centre archives and an unknown anonymous informant interviewed by the OTP who wanted to remain anonymous for security purposes. What is significant, Your Honours, is that this same expert report of Mr. Riedlmayer concludes for entry 169 based on multiple independent sources that there never was any mosque in Kutina village. This is significant because the fourth mosque cited in the indictment for Kalinovik is precisely this non-existent mosque in Kutina. Lest I be accused of getting ahead of myself, the third site in the indictment for Kalinovik is Jesalica mosque, which is not even to be found in the database of Mr. Riedlmayer. So after many years of investigating, the best case the Prosecution can put forth as to Kalinovik is expert evidence which confirms there is no mosque in Kutina at all, damage can be confirmed only to two out of the four mosques as a result of unknown perpetrators, unknown cause, et cetera. Let's now turn to the witnesses. RM034 testified in court on a wholly different topic but was asked in passing about mosques, again very unspecifically. Ms. Bibles at transcript page 1838 through 1839 asks as follows: "Q. Could you tell us whether you're aware of who destroyed the four mosques in Kalinovik? "A. All four mosques in Kalinovik were used before the war except for one of them, the one in Velisi [phoen]. From 1991 to 1995 all three mosques on the territory of the municipality of Kalinovik were torched. The minaret was blown up and the one in the village -- "THE INTERPRETER: The interpreter did not catch the village. The name of the village -- "The witness: [Interpretation] -- and the one in the neighbouring village was also destroyed. "Judge Orie: One minute, Mr. Hadzic. The question and I would like you to focus your answers on what is asked is: Who destroyed the four mosques. Not about how they were destroyed, but who did it. Whether you have any knowledge about it. "Can you answer that question? "The witness: [Interpretation] I do have an answer. It was done by the Serb army." First of all, there is absolutely no identification of any of the mosques that would tie them to those four listed in the indictment. From expert Riedlmayer we know that one of the four never existed, only two of the four were damaged. The testimony of RM034 is thus incapable of belief on this matter. We have nothing that one would expect to establish the prerequisites for a crime. Again, rumour and anonymous hearsay, evidence incapable of belief. RM035 did not testify in these proceedings, but rather a written statement was presented under Rule 92 bis. His statement contains no mention of mosques, as that has been redacted pursuant to adjudicated fact 746. This adjudicated fact taken from the Krajisnik trial judgement merely states that "the mosques of Kalinovik, namely in Ulog, Hotovlje, Kutina, and Jesalica were destroyed during the war." This adjudicated fact is rebutted by the expert report of Riedlmayer because Kutina mosque didn't ever exist. Surely we have not come to a point where the Defence must mount a defence against a Prosecution case that is based solely on an adjudicated fact, which says nothing specific about the manner of damage or destruction or the perpetrators, and which has been refuted as partly untrue by the only expert to testify thus far. Is that within the spirit and meaning of Rule 98 bis to remove such charges at this time? I would argue that the Chamber should remove the same in accord with the purpose and function of the provision. Let's look at Pale, which in the indictment is Schedule D(10) and for which three mosques are to be charged, Praca, Podvitez, and Bogovici. The Prosecution's pre-trial brief, again at page Roman numeral xi of annex B, Schedule D, is unable to provide any identification of alleged perpetrators. One document, 65 ter number 13410, and three witnesses are identified for the supporting evidence on this charge. Your Honours will not be surprised, since I'm bringing it up, the document in question also was not introduced into evidence in this case. One of the witnesses listed is Professor Riedlmayer. Professor Riedlmayer did not offer substantive testimony in court on these three locations in Pale. P2513, his expert report, likewise does not make reference to any of these three locations. Turning to P2511, the database of Professor Riedlmayer, entry 172 is the Praca mosque. Again, the only source is "according to the records of the Islamic community centre ..." and there is not any information about who caused the damage or for what end or purpose. Podvitez mosque is record 173 in P2511, and again the only source is according to the records of the Islamic community centre, and there is not any information about who caused the damage or for what end or purpose. Bogovici mosque is record number 174 in P2511. Again, the only source is the records of the Islamic community centre, and there is not any information about who caused the damage or for what end or purpose. All this is unknown, anonymous hearsay information that does not itself meet the bare minimum to assess criminal liability. Let's look at the witnesses. RM111 who testified at trial was asked in direct examination at transcript page 3148 through 3149 as follows: "Q. And you say in your statement, sir, that you heard after you left the mosques in Pale were destroyed. You referred to the period between July and September 1992. Who controlled Pale at that time? "A. At that time, Pale was under the control of the Serbian Democratic Party." Once again, anonymous hearsay information. This is confirmed in cross-examination at transcript page 3155 that the witness learned all this after the war from unknown others. Again, there is no specification of the perpetrators apart from labelling them as Serb forces. The witness's 92 ter statement P260 at paragraph 79 claims that these mosques were destroyed after the witness left Pale and that the information is "common knowledge" in Pale. Again, rumour and unknown anonymous hearsay. The other witness listed in the Prosecution pre-trial brief for Pale is RM619. Your Honours, RM619 was Ewa Tabeau, the demography expert who offered no evidence as to mosques. So we are left with the evidence that I've already discussed, can barely be called evidence, and surely is not evidence that is capable of belief. Surely it is not the type of case that this Chamber would force the Defence to expend resources to defend against. Your Honours, as our time is limited, I have gone through three of the 11 municipalities in Schedule D and demonstrated the Prosecution case to be deficient as to each. I would ask that you scrutinise the evidence as to each remaining charge and dismiss same if found to be similarly lacking. The Defence has not taken a scatter-gun approach to the charges that it seeks acquittals on simply for the sake of it, rather challenges those that it can show that no evidence capable of supporting a conviction has been proffered by the Prosecution. It is for these types of isolated instances that the charge-based approach is appropriate and the legal veil should be pierced as an exception to the rule, as this approach adheres to the object and purpose of the rule. With this in mind, as the Defence has shown that the Prosecutor has failed to adduce evidence capable of supporting a conviction in relation to the incidents at Jadar River and Sirokaca and Schedule D, it urges the Chamber to enter a judgement of acquittal on these charges to make a clear statement that the allegations that are incapable of sustaining a conviction at this stage will be purged from the indictment to ensure that Defence resources are not squandered, that due process is upheld, and that the Prosecution cannot hide behind a legal veil to surreptitiously push through those allegations for which it has no evidence capable of sustaining a conviction. Following the jurisprudence and adhering to the count-based approach renders the provision worthless and the right of the accused to an acquittal at this stage on charges that the Prosecution has failed to substantiate unobtainable. Today Your Honours have the opportunity to make a clear statement that the provision is more than just one that adheres to the rhetoric of a fair trial. To truly bring war criminals to justice, the trial process must be conducted in a manner that preserves and protects the accused's rights. You have the opportunity to demonstrate that the fight against impunity will not be exploited as a slogan to justify interpreting provisions in a manner that curtails the rights of the accused and a crusade for the Prosecution to hide behind when there is simply no evidence. The indictment at paragraph 34 asserts both Article 7(1) JCE and 7(3) command superior liability against General Mladic for failing to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent and punish crimes alleged to have been committed by VRS forces and so-called Serb forces under his effective control. The indictment at paragraph 12 identifies Serb forces as comprised by members of the Bosnian Serb political and governmental organs, and members of the MUP, VRS, JNA, VJ, TO, the Serbian MUP, Serbian and Bosnian Serb paramilitary forces and volunteer units, and local Bosnian Serbs. In essence, this indictment is not levelled merely at General Mladic, but at every single Serb, an objection that the Defence raised at the preliminary stage as to the lack of specificity and notice compliance under the jurisprudence, resulting from the Prosecution's construction. We would remind of the jurisprudence of the ICTR, the Bagambiki case in 2004, which set a high standard of specificity for JCE in indictments. That Chamber made clear that the Prosecutor must specify in the indictment which form of JCE she argues, the purpose of the enterprise, the identity of the co-perpetrators, and how the accused participated in the enterprise; this was in paragraph 34 of the judgement. Nevertheless, we are still left with this broad definition. We should now look to the evidence that has been presented to try to whittle down this broad allegation to fit the evidence that has been presented for which a case may go -- for which a case may go forward --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I just interrupt you for one second. You referred to paragraph 34 of the indictment, assert --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Bagambiki judgement in 2004, Your Honour, that's ICTR-99-46-T, 25 February 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, the paragraph before that, the indictment at paragraph 34 asserts both Article 7(1) JCE and 7(3) command superior liability against General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the one. I'm wondering, how should we in your view read paragraph 34. Should we read that he failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the commission of crimes, which would mean the commission by others, the others committing the crime either under 7(1) or 7(3); or do you read it that paragraph 34 also includes to charge General Mladic with having committed the crimes under 7(1) himself, any of the modes of liability of 7(1)? And I'm also looking at Mr. Groome perhaps to see whether he has any explanation in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the answer is found in the heading of that section, it's clearly limited to 7(3) of the Statute. 7(1) liability is discussed throughout the entirety of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So in paragraph 34 the reference to 7(1) is primarily to 7(1) liability of those under the command of General Mladic? Or is it just in addition to repeat in every respect that if it's not 7(3) then it certainly is 7(1).

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's the more correct interpretation, Your Honour. Just so that the record is clear, the 7(1) liability also applies to all of the parties -- I think it was paragraph 12 that Mr. Ivetic referred to, where we defined members of the joint criminal enterprise and the people that he implemented their criminal objectives through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That clarifies the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's how I understood it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor -- actually, Your Honours, I think it's time for the break. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is time for the break. We'll take that break. Mr. Ivetic, could you update us on where you are in terms of time. I do understand that out of the four items you would like to bring to our attention -- have we finished the third and are we now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're starting on the third right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the third?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you think you would finish today, which is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As scheduled? That's appreciated. We take the break and we resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Office of the Prosecutor has failed to meet its burden in the indictment or during the course of the trial to specifically identify the subordinates over whom it is alleged that General Mladic had effective de jure or de facto control for whom it is alleged they performed criminal acts for which he is supposed to be responsible. In reference to Srebrenica, paragraphs 21 through 22 of the indictment, the so-called Skorpions unit are added to this laundry list of alleged perpetrator actors over whom General Mladic is alleged to have had effective control or for whose acts he is said to incur liability but limited to their involvement in Trnovo. Paragraph 34(A) of the indictment sets forth that General Mladic failed to initiate investigations into credible allegations of crimes by Serb forces under his effective control. But an accused's position of authority cannot lead to an automatic presumption that he or she knew or had reason to know of the crimes for which a conviction is sought. This is from paragraph 313 of the Delalic appeals judgement. The mental element "had reason to know," as articulated in the Statute, does not automatically imply a duty to obtain information, responsibility can be imposed for deliberately refraining from finding out but not for negligently failing to find out. This is from the Blaskic appeals judgement, paragraph 406. Essentially the Office of the Prosecutor has neither properly pled a sustainable case for the command responsibility element "had reason to know," nor has the evidence established a sustainable case for the same, especially as to non-VRS actors and perpetrators. In this section I ask you at the Rule 98 bis stage to remove the Article 7(1) and 7(3) mode of liability as to charges where the evidence cannot sustain that mode of liability for specific perpetrators. As a preliminary matter, we would point out that there does not appear to have been credible evidence presented by the Prosecution of the involvement of any specified VJ personnel in any of the crimes alleged, let alone evidence of how VJ personnel would be subordinated to General Mladic. As for the other alleged perpetrators, we believe that the Chamber should look at the actual evidence that was presented and appraise whether there is evidence to sustain the burden under Rule 98 bis, demonstrating that actual units of the VRS or under the effective command and control of General Mladic were alleged to have committed crimes for which he is charged or if the evidence is such that other persons, known or unknown, over whom General Mladic did not have effective control are alleged to have committed these crimes according to the evidence. The Prosecution has not adduced any proper evidence that General Mladic issued any criminal orders to individuals who are alleged to have been the perpetrators of the crimes set forth in the indictment. Indeed, as to Srebrenica, Prosecution expert witness Richard Butler confirmed that with respect to July 1995 his research had not come across any document or order from General Mladic specifically ordering the execution of prisoners. This is transcript page 16573 through 16574. It should be recalled that there was only one witness who claimed General Mladic personally participated at one of the sites in Srebrenica, providing cloth to tie the hands of prisoners; that was RM255 at transcript page 1177 through 1178. This is purported to be the 16th of July and was evidence that had not been previously stated by the witness. Your Honours, there has been evidence presented in relation to General Mladic's absence from Bosnia from the 14th to the 16th when he was, among other things, participating in meetings with international negotiators and attending a wedding in Belgrade. Indeed the Prosecution has stipulated as to most of that period of time that General Mladic was far from Srebrenica. And indeed during the testimony of RM255 the Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey in fact, said: "Perhaps one thing that may help. I just wanted to be able to tell the Court that it is not the Prosecution's intention to rely on this most recent evidence related to General Mladic or Karadzic. I wanted to bring that out so that you could see that. I think we've asked him -- perhaps too much of this witness, but we will not be relying upon that." This was transcript page 1179 through 80, right after the witness testified about this alleged personal involvement of General Mladic. So clearly, Your Honours, this type of evidence is not capable of belief. As to the municipalities there has not been evidence capable of belief that indicates General Mladic ever ordered crimes to be committed. I wish to focus on crimes committed by paramilitaries and others that are not in the VRS. First, I will demonstrate that the evidence supports that General Mladic did not have effective control over them, specifically in relation to Arkan's Tigers and the MUP. In several incidents, either the perpetrators were never identified or were identified as paramilitary or police members. The record demonstrates that General Mladic, early on, 28 July 1992, issued an order, P501 in evidence, calling for the disarmament of paramilitaries. This order is critical to show General Mladic's lack of criminal motive and efforts undertaken to try and curb and punish crimes by paramilitaries. This order directs that if intentions of paramilitaries are truly honourable, they should submit themselves to become VRS soldiers subject to control and discipline. For those that have committed crimes, it is said they cannot be taken into the army, but should be disarmed, arrested, and criminal prosecutions started against them. Those that refuse to turn over to army discipline and command but that have not committed crimes are to be arrested and escorted out of the country. It is clear that General Mladic had no hand in the prior actions of these various paramilitaries. Problems effectuating this order are apparent from P5116 dated 17 August 1992, where General Mladic again asks subordinate units why they have not reported on the disarming of paramilitaries pursuant to the aforesaid order. That these groups continued to plague the territory of Republika Srpska beyond the command and control of General Mladic is evidenced by P3095, dated 23 September 1995 with General Mladic complaining to the RS president and the RS police about Arkan's Tigers, considering them a paramilitary that has been operating outside the command of the army and committing crimes, including against loyal Muslims, and asking that the president and police undertake to take action against that group, since it is operating apparently as a member of the MUP police and pursuant to a directive from President Karadzic. Also in evidence we have P5133, dated 26 September 1995, where assistant MUP Minister Kovac and another high-ranking police official seek to meet with General Mladic to resolve "certain problems with regard to the commanding of troops currently under the MUP." Again, from the timing of this document, it is clear who is being talked about. Thereafter we have P5065 dated 19 October 1995, another order coming directly from General Mladic to remove paramilitaries reading as follows: "All paramilitary formations and individuals who refuse subordination in the VRS are to be removed from the territory of the RS by 20 October 1995 at 1200 the latest. "All illegally obtained military technical devices, combat equipment, military and other equipment is to be seized from them and the proper receipts issued to them. "Investigations are to be launched and the proper proceedings initiated for all illegal offences committed, all disciplinary misdemeanours and criminal offences." Again it is clear, not just for Arkan's Tigers but for all paramilitaries, they are not operating with the blessing of General Mladic, nor under his command and control, nor are they undertaking acts intended by General Mladic. Prosecution military expert Theunens testified under oath that Arkan's unit was subordinated to the state security or the DB of the Republic of Serbia. You can find this at transcript page 20683 to 20684. This is corroborated by P3095 which we have just discussed. There has been no evidence suggesting nor establishing by requisite means that General Mladic is the command superior of the Serbian State Security Service of the MUP of Serbia. Accordingly, all charges that have been alleged to be the responsibility of Arkan's Tigers should be dropped from the case at this time as that charge cannot stand. As to other non-VRS actors, it should be recalled that we have in evidence P5052, an order from General Mladic dated 2 July 1992, expressing concern of unauthorised armed persons in uniforms masquerading and operating as if they were officials of the army and police while conducting crimes. This order makes clear the Main Staff only issues written orders, not verbal ones, and that all suspicious units should be checked, while regular units should wear proper uniforms, and that units should prevent such impersonators from engaging in combat unless they pass security checks and submit to be incorporated into the army as regular soldiers. Let's talk about MUP forces themselves. In relation to the events in Srebrenica and indeed municipalities, there has been some evidence presented by the Prosecution that the members of the MUP had been responsible for crimes that are alleged against General Mladic. Some instances that come to mind are the killings in Kravica and the killings at Trnovo. From the foregoing documentation as to paramilitaries, we see that General Mladic did not have effective command and control over these units when the same were operating under the auspices of the MUP. The same result is true for civilian MUP police, once they have finished operating in combat operations. Returning to expert Theunens, this Prosecution expert explained the concept in the SFRY military of "Sadejestvo," or "co-ordinated" action during operations, where two forces operated alongside one another without actual subordination. This is transcript page 20616 through 20617. Mr. Theunens further explained the concept of resubordination or reattachment of the MUP to VRS army units for limited purposes; transcript page 20621. Mr. Theunens described that once combat operations are done, the police returns to their police function and their police superiors, and thereafter the VRS army commanders in the region can only thereafter report MUP wrongdoing to the police authorities and the MUP superiors have the responsibility of any further disciplinary or other actions. This is transcript page 20622 through 20625. Your Honours, we have seen General Mladic do precisely that in relation to Arkan's unit. He did all that a military leader can do with relation to police personnel not under his authority. We think that under these circumstances the crimes alleged to be committed by MUP members alone, such as Kravica warehouse, must be dismissed from the case as to General Mladic. Indeed, OTP investigator Blaszczyk confirmed the Petrovic video which follows the actions of police units around Srebrenica and part of the scene at Kravica. Mr. Blaszczyk confirmed that General Mladic is not seen anywhere in relation to that video. This is at transcript page 12373. One further thing I would like to point out, the so-called Skorpions group at Trnovo, the infamous video of their killing of six individuals; P2581 is that video. It was played numerous times by the Prosecution. However gruesome the video and however repulsive and reprehensible the actions of these Skorpions, they have nothing to do with General Mladic. OTP investigator Janc testified that Mladic is neither present in any part of the Skorpion video nor is he mentioned by the perpetrators therein as having any role in the killings. This is transcript page 15378. The best testimony before this Chamber that is suited to illuminate the events in Trnovo was very explicit and resounding in clearing General Mladic of any involvement in this crime. The evidence is clear the Skorpion perpetrators never mentioned General Mladic, but rather always were clear their superiors were the Serbian DB and the MUP assistant minister for Serb Krajina. This can be found at transcript reference 18710 through 18711. The evidence as to Trnovo is also clear. The Skorpion unit itself was operating in co-ordinated action as described by Mr. Theunens rather than being resubordinated to the VRS. This is at transcript page 18715 through 18717. The perpetrators from the Skorpions themselves were not engaged in co-ordinated action with the VRS at the time of the crime, but rather were described as body-guards, a driver, a mechanic, and a member of the kitchen staff engaged in personal acts. This is at transcript page 18729 through 18730. The evidence is clear these perpetrators have been tried and are serving sentences in Serbia. There is no role of General Mladic in ordering or taking part in these killings in any way. The perpetrators were not subordinated to him, thus he could not discipline them. There has been no evidence of how General Mladic ought to have known of the crimes. Accordingly, this charge should be dismissed. Another topic that I wish to raise at this point is Tomasica, which we have heard the Prosecution claim is a mass grave that Mladic's own notebooks confess culpability in. Respectfully, P358, page 154 in e-court, the notebook cited by the Prosecution in question, does not support the Prosecution's case. In it, Mladic is being told of a police official's comments as to Tomasica. General Mladic makes clear the VRS knows nothing about those bodies, that the police may be trying to pass their own misdeeds to them. General Mladic directs that investigations be carried out as to those bodies. Again, for crimes committed by persons from the police, outside of his effective control, this evidence cannot lead to criminal responsibility for Mladic as the VRS Main Staff commander. Turning to the incident at Schedule A(7.5) of the indictment, Skrljevita, spelled S-k-r-l-j-e-v-i-t-a, one witness was called in relation to the same, Grgo Stojic. Your Honours will recall that during the testimony of this witness, it was revealed that the perpetrators of this crime never once mentioned General Mladic; this is transcript page 4125 through 4126. Further, it was demonstrated by the witness himself that the principal perpetrators of the same were aged 15 and 17 years respectively at the time of the commission, which leads to the conclusion they were not VRS soldiers. And that the other alleged perpetrator arrested and prosecuted by the authorities in Republika Srpska could not in fact be identified by this witness. This is at transcript page 4112 through 4120. Indeed, at transcript page 4109 through 4110, the witness confirmed the Banja Luka military court already in November 1992 ordered that all alleged perpetrators be taken into custody for the murder and investigations launched -- for the murder and that investigations be launched, all this shortly after the crime occurred. At transcript page 4110 through -11, the witness confirmed that the military police of the VRS identified the perpetrators, including minors who were outside the army, and conducted an on-site investigation. Exhibit P369 is the indictment that was raised by the military court against the perpetrators, condemning the crime. Your Honours, there is thus no credible evidence of belief that persons subordinated to and under the effective command and control of General Mladic could be said to have committed this crime or that military organs under his control failed to investigate and prosecute the perpetrators. Accordingly, this charge should be dismissed. I have highlighted concrete and clear examples. For the record, the Prosecution case as presented involved paramilitaries or MUP personnel as perpetrators as to the following Schedule A incidents: 3.3, Kljuc; 6.7 and 6.8, Prijedor; 9.1, Vlasenica. The Prosecution evidence fails to particularly identify the perpetrators or differentiate amongst them as to the following incidents from Schedule A: 6.1, Prijedor; 6.5 to 6.6, Prijedor; 6.9, Prijedor; 7.3, Sanski Most. The Prosecution case as presented involves paramilitaries or MUP personnel as perpetrators, as to the following Schedule B incidents: 1.1, Sanski Most; 1.2, Sanski Most; 10.1 and 10.2, Novi Grad; 13.1 to 13.4, Prijedor; 16.2, Vlasenica. Meanwhile, the evidence fails to particularly identify the perpetrators or differentiate them as to the following from Schedule B, 2.1, Bijeljina. As to detention centres, the Defence points out that Omarska and Keraterm were police facilities. Based on the evidence presented, the Prosecution case cannot stand as to these charges. General Mladic is reputed to be a key member and/or principal perpetrator in an overarching joint criminal enterprise lasting from October 1991 until 30 November 1995, with the objective to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from Bosnian Serb acclaimed territory. This is paragraph 5 of the indictment. The indictment sets out an additional but related joint criminal enterprise aimed at eliminating the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica and spreading terror among civilians in Sarajevo; this is paragraph 6 of the indictment. General Mladic is alleged to share the intent for the commission of genocide, persecution, extermination, murder, deportations, and forcible transfer with other members of this joint criminal enterprise; this is paragraph 8 of the indictment. Alternatively, General Mladic purportedly could foresee that the crime of genocide might be perpetrated by one or more members of this joint criminal enterprise and willingly took this risk; that's paragraph 9 of the indictment. The Defence challenges the evidentiary base presented by the Prosecution in relation to the mode of liability, a third category of joint criminal enterprise, for purpose of a no-case submission under Rule 98 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Our position is that the Prosecution has not presented sufficient evidence to render a conviction supporting the charge that General Mladic shared or intended to further the common purpose of the JCE. The Defence would like to remind Your Honours of the separate and dissenting opinions of Judges Hunt and Bennouna in the Celebici case: "The fundamental function of the criminal law is to punish the accused for his criminal conduct, and only for his criminal conduct. We believe that taking into account abstract elements creates the danger the accused will also be convicted of additional crimes which have a distinct existence only as a purely legal and abstract manner, effectively through the historical accidents of the way in which humanitarian law has developed in streams having distinct contextual requirements. The fact that the articles of the Statute encompass different, although frequently overlapping, crimes is a result mainly of the history of international humanitarian law rather than any indication that they are intended to describe genuinely distinct bodies of criminal law in contemporary international humanitarian law." Before this Tribunal, the Tadic Appeals Chamber stipulated that it is only appropriate to apply the notion of common purpose in relation to a joint criminal enterprise where the following requirements concerning mens rea are fulfilled by the accused: One, the intention to take part in a JCE and to further, individually and jointly, the criminal purpose of this enterprise; and two, the foreseeability of the possible commission by other members of the group of offences that do not constitute the object of the common criminal purpose. That's paragraph 220 of the Tadic appeals judgement. With your leave, Your Honours, I will address evidence relating to the requirement that General Mladic willingly entered into the joint criminal enterprise and supposedly shared and furthered the common purpose of the same. Subsequently I will address evidence relating to the requirement that General Mladic could foresee the crime of genocide being committed. We submit that the Prosecution has not shown that the accused willingly entered into the joint criminal enterprise. The mere position General Mladic held within the VRS cannot be used as primary evidence to infer his criminal responsibility, doing so would militate against the principle of personal guilt. Rather than distinguishing between the accused and the specific crimes for which he stands trial, this concept degenerates into a smoke-screen which obscures the frail connection between General Mladic and the acts for which he stands trial. An accused's position of authority cannot lead to an automatic presumption that he or she knew or had reason to know of the crimes for which a conviction is sought. That is again from the Delalic appeals judgement, paragraph 313 and again from Blaskic appeals paragraph 406, the mental element "had reason to know" does not automatically imply a duty to obtain information. Responsibility can be imposed for deliberately refraining from finding out but not for negligently failing to find out. Essentially the OTP has neither properly pled a sustainable case nor has the evidence established a sustainable case for the same. We submit that the Prosecution has not proven that General Mladic agreed or supported the common purpose of the third category of JCE in relation to the crime of genocide. The Defence recognises that the proper scope of JCE III is not completely settled in international criminal law. This is supported by Judge Shahabuddeen's conclusion to his separate opinion in the Brdjanin appeals judgement: "... a physical perpetrator has to be a member of the JCE for a member of the latter to be criminally responsible for a crime perpetrated by the physical perpetrator within the common purpose of the JCE. By predicating the need for an agreement expressive of the intention of the parties, that position respect the essentials of the principle that criminal responsibility is only assigned for one's own conduct ..." An agreement expressive of the intention of the parties, as referenced to by Judge Shahabuddeen, requires the Prosecution to prove that the accused by his acts or acquiescence is part of such a JCE agreement. This is paragraph 4 of Judge Shahabuddeen's dissenting opinion. The Krajisnik Trial Chamber held that persons in a criminal enterprise must have engaged in concerted action; this is the Krajisnik Trial Chamber judgement in paragraph 884 and is also referenced in the Krajisnik Appeals Chamber judgement at paragraph 192 through 194. The Defence recognises that it is established case law before this Tribunal to render convictions under the third category of joint criminal enterprise for specific intent crimes such as genocide. Nevertheless, we would like to give notice to Judge Liu's recent partially dissenting opinion and declaration to the Sainovic appeals judgement. Judge Liu recognised that genocide requires that the perpetrator's intent goes beyond the mere prohibited and that as a consequence the mens rea required for specific intent crimes is incompatible with the standard of advertent recklessness applied to a third category joint criminal enterprise. In the absence of evidence of specific genocidal intent, no conviction of genocide may be entered. Furthermore, Judge Liu finds the words of Antonio Cassese persuasive: "Whoever is liable under the third category of JCE has a distinct mens rea from that of the 'primary offender.' Nevertheless, as the 'secondary offender' bears responsibility for the same crime as the primary offender, the 'distance' between the subjective element of the two offenders must not be so dramatic as in the case of crimes requiring specific intent. Otherwise, the crucial notions of 'personal culpability' and 'causation' would be torn to shreds." And indeed a further discussion of this can be found in Cassese's book: "Limits of Individual Criminal Responsibility under the Doctrine of JCE," pages 121 to 122. The Defence submits that in light of Judge Liu's dissenting decision, the Prosecution has not provided enough evidence to point out General Mladic's specific intent and therefore he's entitled to a dismissal of the related charge. Evidence shows General Mladic did not share intent related to any common purpose that has been identified by the Prosecution. Prosecution witness Manojlo Milovanovic in his testimony on 19 September 2013 attested to that fact. His testimony pertained to directive 7, a directive issued and signed by the supreme commander, Mr. Karadzic. General Milovanovic explains that unit commanders should not take any measures based on directives from Karadzic which should have been sent to General Mladic instead. In this particular instance, directive 7 was sent to all the corps commands. This was an instance of duality or double lines in the chain of command. Corps commanders should not have reacted to Karadzic's directive before receiving Mladic's orders as a result of the directive. The task assignment to the Drina Corps by General Mladic in directive 7.1 was not taken over from directive 7. The general left two things out in directive 7: The first is the controversial sentence that unbearable conditions have to be created for the civilian population of Zepa and Srebrenica; the second element left out is the sentence referring to the separation of Srebrenica and Zepa by force. General Milovanovic states that the accused exercised personal responsibility when he decided not to pressure the civilian population, and thereby not adopt every element from Karadzic's directive 7. This clearly shows that General Mladic did not share in any nefarious intent that could be attributed as arising out of directive 7. In addition, Exhibit P3095 relating to General Mladic's demand to withdraw Karadzic's authorisation to the paramilitary formation Arkan's Tigers, this evidence shows that the accused did not share any nefarious intent that could be attributed to Karadzic or other alleged JCE members. The demand specifically mentions the arrest and abuse of non-Serbs and requests the MUP to take measures for the crimes they committed and to disarm this formation, which was operating pursuant to authorisation issued by Supreme Commander Karadzic. Your Honours, evidence shows that the accused did not share the intent and common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from Bosnian Serb acclaimed territory and our position is that the Prosecution has not presented sufficient evidence to the contrary. Furthermore, the Defence would like to remind Your Honours of the difference between commander responsibility liability and liability under the head of a third category JCE, as clarified in the Brdjanin Appeals Chamber and to keep that in mind when deliberating over this evidence. As outlined before, the Defence will now address evidence relating to the requirement that General Mladic could foresee the crime of genocide being committed by other alleged members of the JCE. The Tadic Appeals Chamber stated that everyone in the joint criminal enterprise must have been able to predict this result. It notes that more than negligence is required. The standard applied to the third category of a JCE is that of dolus eventualis. Lack of agreement between the members of the JCE risks that one or more of the perpetrators goes outside of the purview of the common purpose of the enterprise. A JCE warrants a common understanding and mutual attribution of the conduct of the participants and our position is that the JCE doctrine is not the appropriate instrument to sustain a conviction of General Mladic's alleged genocidal intent nor has the Prosecution presented sufficient evidence in this matter. We believe this position to be in line with the reasoning of the Kvocka Appeals Chamber judgement at paragraphs 91 through 92. The indictment alleges that General Mladic was aware or could foresee a genocide happening. The Tadic Appeals Chamber dealt with the same matter and stated that "uncertainty in the mind went to the question whether genocide would in fact be committed not to acceptance by him of it (if and when it was committed) as something which he could 'predict' as the 'natural and foreseeable consequence' of the activities of the joint criminal enterprise to which he was a party." It is important for purposes of our 98 bis submission in relation to foreseeability that General Mladic's intent to commit the crime of genocide must be shown to include the specific intent to commit genocide even when he did not know whether or not genocide would be committed. I would like to remind Your Honours that Tadic was not convicted of the crime of genocide. Furthermore, the Tadic appeals judgement stated that it is still necessary to show intent and that this was shown by the particular circumstances surrounding the JCE. Former Judge Cassese shared his view on foreseeability. He was of the opinion that the foreseeability standard is neither precise nor reliable. It almost introduces a form of strict liability, as it will be for the Prosecution to prove that the participant had knowledge and willing took that risk of a specific fact or circumstance, evincing the likelihood that the other participant might commit a unconcerted crime. Furthermore he stated that: "Clearly, if the Prosecution fails to prove all this, the charge must be dismissed. It would be contrary to the principles of a fair trial to shift the burden of proof and to require the Defence to prove that the accused did not know the relevant facts nor foresee the crime and willingly took risk that it be committed." Again, this is from page 117 of "Proper Limits of Individual Criminal Liability under the Doctrine of JCE," a publication by former Judge Cassese. In his dissenting opinion to the Brdjanin interlocutory appeal decision, it is said: "... the third category of joint criminal enterprise does not dispense with the need to prove intent: What it does is that it provides a mode of proving intent in particular circumstances, namely, by proof of foresight in those circumstances." And again we're talking about Judge Shahabuddeen, paragraphs 4 through 5 of his separate opinion. In light of the common understanding and mutual attribution of the conduct of the participants and the particular circumstances surrounding the JCE, the Defence would like to draw Your Honours' attention to Exhibit P4283, a decision by Supreme Commander Karadzic. The decision pertains to Karadzic's attempt to reassign Mladic to a position outside of the Main Staff. This attempt is corroborated by Prosecution Witness General Milovanovic. Your Honours, I would like to quote page 17106 of the transcript, where Milovanovic says: "Karadzic started about speaking renaming the Main Staff into the General Staff. I asked him -- actually, I asked him whether all of those present should be listening, and he said that everybody else should leave except for Krajisnik, and then he said to me, General, we are renaming the Main Staff into the General Staff. General Mladic will be replaced and he will be the special adviser for defence for Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serb Krajina. And I shot back by way of a response saying that I would not be head of that General Staff. Krajisnik added, Radovan, let him be now. This is an initial action on the spur-of-the-moment. As a soldier, he will have to receive his orders. The order did arrive the next day. Again, I refused it even in writing; that is to say, all generals of Republika Srpska refused and signed a petition to the Assembly of Republika Srpska. It was the Assembly that appointed Ratko Mladic as head of the Main Staff, so it is only the Assembly that can relieve him of that duty, not the president." Based on the foregoing, the most reasonable conclusion on the evidence is that there was no common understanding of the type alleged by the Prosecution and the attempt of President Karadzic to reassign Mladic is highly indicative in the circumstances of the alleged JCE that tried to exclude the accused. Our position is that the Prosecution has not proven sufficient evidence to prove otherwise. I think we're at the time for a break. We could take one now before moving to my last comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this would be a suitable moment for you, we'll take the break now. We take a break and we'll resume at 25 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you're ready to proceed, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours, thank you. I would like to point out to Your Honours other evidence that speaks against any specific genocidal intent on the part of General Mladic. I would direct your attention to the transcript of the 16th Assembly Session held on 12 May 1992 in which supreme commander and President Karadzic formulated six strategic goals for the Serbian people. The Prosecution has presented its view that President Karadzic formulated and promoted the development and implementation of SDS and Bosnian Serb governmental policies intended to advance the objective of the joint criminal enterprise and that the six strategic objectives are proof of concerted action within the JCE. Our position is the same as that of the Chamber in the Sikirica case. The Trial Chamber of the Sikirica case found that general political doctrine of the Serb leadership, including the six strategic goals, propagated persecutions in Prijedor directed against the non-Serb community, but found no evidence the general political doctrine carried any genocidal intent. The Stakic and Krajisnik Chambers came to the same conclusion. We argue that the Prosecution has not presented any new evidence to overrule such a conclusion. In addition, per the evidence on the record, General Mladic specifically was opposed to the adoption of the six strategic goals at the Assembly and said: "We have to call upon any man who has bowed his forehead to the ground to embrace these areas and the territory of the state we plan to make. He too has his place with us and next to us ..." And he goes on further to say: "... but that does not mean that Muslims have to be expelled or drowned ..." This fragment clearly shows that he does not share the intent nor common purpose of this alleged third category of joint criminal enterprise. In this Assembly dated 12 May 1992 in Banja Luka, Mladic clearly states his intent to live together with Bosnian Muslims and repudiates the concept that Muslims have to be expelled or drowned. The absence of his intent, which the Defence would like to stress, is separate from that of other members implicated in the JCE is corroborated by Witness Donia's testimony. During his testimony, Donia emphasised Mladic issued harsh warnings against taking actions stipulated by the Serb political leadership in the 16th Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please slow down a bit, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, he acknowledged that Mladic made a number of statements expressing his concern that the political leadership was formulating goals that entailed Serbs ruling over areas where no Serbs lived. This is the 22nd August 2013 testimony of Mr. Donia. P2141 dated 25 October 1995, in which the VRS Main Staff security department authorised subordinate units to engage in exchange of Muslim prisoners with the Muslim side for Serb prisoners clearly negates any possibility that Mladic's intent was to destroy the protected group of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. Similarly, P2142, dated 16 June 1994 and P2143 dated 21 January 1995 also demonstrate that the VRS Main Staff security department authorised negotiations for exchange of Muslim prisoners for Serb prisoners. Furthermore, we have in evidence P8167, dated 20 July 1995, which -- in which it records a meeting between the UN and General Mladic, who clearly conveys his intention to exchange all prisoners in custody of the VRS with the Muslim side for all their prisoners. Your Honours, we have several exhibits pertaining to the fact General Mladic was in favour of a complete cessation of hostilities agreement and a peace agreement. There is Exhibit P2198 dated 17 June 1995 which accounts the meeting between General Mladic and General Janvier in which General Mladic says he's in favour of completing the agreement and is willing to do a cease-fire across the whole territory. Similarly, P2050 dated 14 March 1995 records a meeting between Akashi, Mladic, and talks of the other side breaching the cessation of hostilities agreement while the Serb side has adhered to it. In addition, P332, dated 30 May 1992, pertaining to General Mladic's meeting with Colonel Wilson with a purpose of getting the UN to organise a meeting with the BH side to discuss a cease-fire in Sarajevo as the BH side has been refuting such attempts. And lastly, P18 dated 12 January 1995, where Mladic specifically agrees to complete the cessation of hostilities agreement with the other two sides. Your Honours, I would like to proceed with addressing the crime of genocide under Count 1 and subsequently under Count 2. We respectfully seek to challenge the Prosecution's evidentiary basis and submit that it has been deficient in meeting the reduced burden of proof set by Rule 98 bis --

utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if by any chance you would have the source of the quote of the Banja Luka Assembly Session, then it would assist me. If not, then I would not be surprised if you don't have all the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- we can get that before we finish today, Your Honour.
