utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Genocide is punishable under Article 4 of the ICTY Statute and is a well-established part of customary international law. As underlined in many international trials, genocide is distinct from other crimes inasmuch as it embodies a special intent or dolus specialis. This is from the Kayishema judgement, paragraph 498. To sustain a count of genocide, the perpetrator has to possess the required mens rea. Genocidal intent requires an extra element besides the mental element, mirroring the genocidal acts allegedly committed by the accused. The additional required specific genocidal intent consists of three elements: Namely, the intent to destroy the protected group; the intent to destroy the group in whole or in part; and this protected group is either defined by nationality, ethnicity, religion, or race. Previous Trial Chambers have emphasised that intent is a mental factor which is difficult, even impossible, to determine. These presumptions are formed on a case-by-case basis and rely on the evidence put forward during trial. The Akayesu trial judgement paragraph 523 through 524. Absent a finding of specific genocidal intent, the acts cannot be tried as genocide but inevitably fall within a different category of international crimes, for instance, a crime against humanity. Absent a confession or direct evidence attesting to the accused's intent, presumptions on intent are formed on a case-by-case basis and are inferred from the material evidence submitted to the Chamber. This is from the Musema trial judgement, paragraph 167. The Defence submits, in line with the arguments regarding the actus reus, that the Prosecution evidence currently supporting inferences of intent of the accused is not sufficient to meet the Rule 98 bis standard. With your leave, Your Honours, I will first turn to the actus reus element that General Mladic is charged with under Count 1 and then turn to the mental elements. Count 1 alleges the commission of genocide in the municipalities of Foca, Kljuc, Kotor Varos, Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Vlasenica; this is in paragraph 37 in the indictment. The indictment holds that a campaign of persecutions included or escalated to conduct manifesting intent to destroy in part the national, ethnical and/or religious groups of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. In these seven municipalities, the intent to partially destroy the groups was manifested through the targeting of significant sections of the leadership and a substantial number of its members. This is also paragraph 37. The genocidal acts subsumed in Count 1 are: (A) the killing of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats; (B) the causing of serious bodily or mental harm to Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats during their confinement in detention facilities; and (C) the detention of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats under conditions of life calculated to bring about their physical destruction. Your Honours, no evidence has been presented to substantiate a general factual finding of genocide in the municipalities. Demographer and Prosecution expert Tabeau presented evidence which shows that 2.6 per cent of Muslims were killed in Bosnia. Tabeau's testimony on 18 November 2013 stated that the Bosnian Serbs lost the highest percentage of their population, some -- as opposed to the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat population and Ms. Tabeau testified that there was in fact only a small difference in losses among the ethnic groups. The Defence is aware that a determination of genocide does not exclusively involve a numerical assessment, but that it is of guidance. We would like to respectfully bring to Your Honours' mind the ICJ judgement concerning the application of the convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina versus Serbia and Montenegro, 26 February 2007, which was not satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the killings of members of the protected group in 1992 were carried out with genocidal intent. ICJ judgements are not binding on the Trial Chamber but are of an authoritative nature. Your Honours, before this Tribunal several cases have examined the occurrence of genocide as alleged in the municipalities; none of them have established it. The Trial Chamber in Stakic found no special genocidal intent to destroy the protected group of Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats. The Trial Chamber in Stakic was not satisfied that anyone had the special intent to destroy the Muslims or Croats as a group and they specifically discussed the strategic goals and found that they called for separation, not destruction. The Stakic Appeals Chamber upheld the acquittal of genocide and ascertained that there was insufficient evidence supporting the proposition the Serb leadership developed a genocidal campaign. The Trial Chamber of the Sikirica case found that general political doctrine of the Serb leadership propagated persecutions, but found no evidence that general political doctrine carried any genocidal intent. The Defence again likes to state our position that the Prosecution has not presented any new evidence in this case that would result in any different conclusion than prior cases. Furthermore, the Chamber recognised in Stakic that the Serbs had the structures in place to commit genocide if they intended to do so. The Stakic Trial Chamber acknowledged that while approximately 23.000 people were registered as having passed through Trnopolje camp, the total number of killings in Prijedor probably did not exceed 3.000. Similarly, Your Honours, the Tribunal had before it the case of Krajisnik, who was accused of committing genocide on a national level and included the seven municipalities contained in Count 1. The Krajisnik Chamber found that no genocide occurred and could not establish the presence of genocidal intent. The Appeals Chamber of Brdjanin upheld their acquittal of genocide as the Chamber found no evidence of the intent to destroy the protected group. Furthermore, the Brdjanin Chamber specifically mentioned the absence of an escalation to genocide in the ARK after examining the killings at Koricanske Stijene, killings and treatment of prisoners at Keraterm, Omarska, Trnopolje, and Prijedor, Kljuc, and Sanski Most. Your Honours, before I continue, I can report that the 16th Assembly Session is in evidence at P431. The quote of General Mladic is to be found at page 39 of the English translation as the document is uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If Your Honours would allow me to make reference to the genocide in Rwanda, where after repetitively inquiring into the existence of genocide in Rwanda, the events were referred to as common knowledge in further trials after 2006. The Karemera case confirmed that the societal context in which the accused operated has direct bearing on the charges brought against him. This is paragraph 36 of the decision on the Prosecutor's interlocutory appeal on the decision of judicial notice, June 16th, 2006. Notwithstanding that sole reference on a general finding of genocide would go contrary to individual criminal responsibility and would lead to adjudicating guilt by association. Instead, evidence is viewed in light of the larger societal context in which the alleged actions took place. The position of the Defence is that there has not been proven genocide occurred in the municipalities between 31 March 1992 and 31 December 1992 and that the Prosecution has not submitted evidence to the contrary. The evidence should be viewed in light of the larger societal context in which the alleged actions took place. In absence of direct evidence that the physical perpetrators of the crimes alleged to have been committed in the municipalities carried out these crimes with genocidal intent, the Chamber can infer intent. While the Chamber has heard evidence of culpable acts directed against Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats in the municipalities and the repetition of derogatory language; however, the nature, scale, and context of these acts, be it all -- be it in all the municipalities covered by the indictment or the seven municipalities in which genocide is alleged, do not reach the level from which a reasonable trier of fact can infer that they were committed with genocidal intent. The Karadzic Appeals Chamber remarked that forcible transfer does not constitute a genocidal act in and of itself, but where attended by such circumstances as to lead to the death of the whole or part of the displaced population, it may be considered an underlying offence that causes serious bodily or mental harm. This is also emphasised by the Krstic and Popovic Chambers. Your Honours, I would like to remind you that bodily harm or mental harm imposed to fall within the crime of genocide must be committed with the intent to destroy the protected group as such. The Trial Chamber in the Kayishema case established that an accused cannot be held liable for the mental injury inflicted upon victims if it is not inflicted whilst harbouring specific genocidal intent to destroy the protected group, that's paragraph 112 of the Kayishema trial judgement. By deciding so, the ICTR set precedent that restricts the crime of genocide and consequently puts an elevated burden of proof on the Prosecution. We submit the Prosecution has not presented sufficient evidence to prove that General Mladic harboured specific genocidal intent and therefore he is entitled to a dismissal of the charge in relation to inflicting mental harm. The Prosecution asserts that the common purpose of the JCE was implemented through the various VRS directives. Again, we would like to stress the testimony of General Milovanovic pertaining to directive 7, in which General Mladic left two things out that were authorised by President Karadzic in his own directive 7.1. The first is the controversial sentence about unbearable conditions needing to be created for the civilian population of Zepa and Srebrenica. The second referring to the separation of Srebrenica and Zepa or from Zepa by force. Therefore, General Mladic could not have been said to share the same common purpose, let alone the common purpose to commit genocide. The indictment charges General Mladic with crimes committed against the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica commencing the days preceding 11 July 1995 and continuing until 1 November 1995. General Mladic is alleged to have participated in a joint criminal enterprise to eliminate the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica by killing the men and boys of Srebrenica and forcibly removing the women, young children, and elderly, amounting to the commission of the crime of genocide. The key proof that the Prosecution relies upon as to General Mladic's intent pertaining to the events in Srebrenica is witness Kingori. However, this evidence is incapable of belief, due to the fact that Kingori's other evidence as to the Srebrenica enclave is entirely at odds with members of UNPROFOR. Whereas Kingori testified that the evacuation of civilians was staged by the VRS, General Nicolai confirmed - of the United Nations and the Dutch Ministry of Defence - agreed the evacuation was a humanitarian necessity and instructed Colonel Karremans to ask Mladic to permit it during his first meeting at Hotel Fontana. This is transcript page 10653 through 10654. Thus, the actions relating to deportation cannot be attributed to General Mladic, not unless the United Nations and Dutch Ministry of Defence themselves are the co-perpetrators of the same. Furthermore, it should be recalled that whereas Kingori claimed that the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica were completely demilitarised, this account is at odds with DutchBat witnesses who testified, including Eelco Koster at transcript page 1266 through 1267 and 1278 to 1279 and also to evidence of armed Bosnian Muslims taking UN members hostages, Witness van Duijn at transcript page 6281 and Witness Koster at transcript page 1240. This evidence shows that the Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica were not demilitarised and even threatened DutchBat themselves. Thus, Kingori's testimony is not one that is capable of belief. Prosecution expert, Richard Butler, confirmed, as we said earlier, that with respect to July 1995 in Srebrenica, his research had not come across any document or order from General Mladic specifically ordering the execution of prisoners; this is transcript page 16573 to 16574. Your Honours, the Defence would like to remind that the Prosecution in its opening statement confirmed and conceded that the military action of the VRS against Srebrenica to stop Armija BiH raids constituted a legitimate military action. This can be found at transcript page 486. Later Prosecution expert witness Richard Butler confirmed this assessment. Likewise, Butler confirmed that VRS combat operations against the Bosnian Muslim column leaving Susnjari was likewise legitimate combat. This can be found at transcript page 16653. Butler states that: "I don't see any particular conflict with respect to the column retreating from Srebrenica and fighting its way to friendly lines." He goes on to state: "As I've testified many times before, the column as constituted, despite the fact that the mixed character of the column, in my view the column constituted a legitimate military target which meant it was subject to attack by ambush." In addition, we would like to submit that there is no evidence of General Mladic's presence at any of the alleged execution sites, save for the testimony of RM255, which we have already addressed and which even the Prosecution has said they do not intend for us to rely upon. And again that's at transcript page 1179. Further, the evidence is clear and the Prosecution stipulated to the fact that General Mladic has left the Srebrenica area and left the VRS zone of operations as of 14 July 1995. Although the precise time of his return is still in dispute between the parties, it -- from the evidence it is clear the killings that took place took place while General Mladic was not present. The Prosecution has not presented evidence that General Mladic had any capabilities of secure communications during this time-period, either with the VRS units or other alleged JCE members, so as to permit his knowledge of or participation in the killings. The Karadzic Appeals Chamber in its 98 bis decision in reinstating the genocide count for the municipalities focused on the detention facilities being used to subject conditions of life meant to bring about physical destruction. In the Srebrenica context, we do not have such evidence. To the contrary, we have presented evidence that prisoner exchanges were planned. We elaborated on Exhibit P2141, dated 25 October 1995, in which the VRS Main Staff security department authorises subordinates to engage in exchange of Muslim prisoners. Similarly, Exhibit P2142, dated 16 June 1994, and Exhibit P2143, dated 21 January 1995, which also demonstrate the intent to exchange Muslim prisoners for Serb prisoners. And then again the 20 July 1995, P816, where General Mladic conveys his intention to exchange all prisoners for all prisoners. I would like to remind Your Honours also in relation to the standard set forth in the Kayishema case that an accused cannot be held liable for mental injury inflicted upon victims if it is not inflicted whilst harbouring specific genocidal intent to destroy the protected group, that on 14 July 1995 General Mladic's meeting with General Smith of UNPROFOR and agrees to permit the International Red Cross to come examine prisoners from Srebrenica to assure they are kept in accord with the Geneva Conventions. This is D410. This evidence flies in the face of the assumption that General Mladic's alleged intent was to inflict bodily and mental harm to the detainees with the genocidal intent. Further, as early as April 1994 we have evidence of General Mladic meeting with General Wahlgren of the UN and offering the following three proposals for Srebrenica, this is P2469: "(A) the UN could send as many empty trucks as it wanted into Srebrenica to take out Muslims or. "(B) if the Muslim commander in Srebrenica (Naser Oric) does not allow his people to leave in this manner, the Serb side could open a corridor allowing civilians to cross into Serb-held territory (on foot) to a place where they can board buses; or. "(C) as civilians were not the target of the BH Serb army, the Muslims could lay down their arms and let their people stay in Srebrenica. The Muslims in Srebrenica, he said, should 'surrender to my forces or yours. However, according to international law they should surrender to ours.' "He asked that this proposal be transmitted to the other side." The Defence would like to also turn to statements made by General Mladic at Hotel Fontana which must be taken in the context of his statements a year prior as we just evidenced in the meeting with General Wahlgren. Taken in context with these prior statements, it is clear that General Mladic's focus is the armed 5.000 or so fighters of Naser Oric that he thinks are still with the civilians and that if disarmed no one has to leave Srebrenica. Such a benign interpretation of his words is in line with his statements to the crowd at Potocari, which can be seen at P1147, page 55 through 56, and this is General Mladic talking: "Well, I have received the representatives of this population here, today, and they have asked me to enable the civilians who want to leave this territory to pass on the territory controlled by Muslims and Croats. Our army wasn't aiming to fight the civilians or the UNPROFOR forces. We have organised the transport for them, the food, the water, the medicine. In the first round today, we will evacuate women, children, and the old, as well as other people who want to leave this combat area on their own free will, without any kind of force. "Yes, Srebrenica is free, but as I said to their representatives they should all ... there are still groups ... which are fighting, there is still resistance. I also ordered that their soldiers could join us freely and surrender their weapons and they accepted it. I hope at least this part of the problem can be solved by us without civilians being hurt and these women and children and the old ... it's not their fault if Alija and his policy seduced them." Furthermore, we would like to bring to Your Honours' attention the testimony of RM253 regarding another speech attributed to General Mladic at Sandici. The speech clearly shows that General Mladic's intent is not geared towards the destruction of the protected group of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, but rather is aimed towards prisoner exchanges because he says everyone will be exchanged; this is P1547 under seal at paragraph 20. Further, key Prosecution witness Erdemovic testified at transcript page 13779 that he never heard any talk or any indicators that the objective of the VRS was to destroy the protected group of Bosniak people. We submit that the Prosecution has not proven sufficient evidence to the contrary. On the matter of genocidal intent for purposes of this 98 bis hearing, the Defence would like to conclude that it is aware that the Courts entertain freedom of assessment of evidence. And we would like to recall the Jelisic case in which the accused publicly displayed his intent to destroy the Muslim group in whole or in part through making statements as feeling the need to kill 20 to 30 persons before being able to drink his coffee each morning. However, he also granted Muslim detainees amnesty, a notorious example being a Muslim man who was forced to engage in Russian roulette with Mr. Jelisic and who was subsequently released. In weighing the evidence the Court put significant emphasis on the latter exculpatory evidence which lead to finding that due to the uncertainty surrounding his intent to destroy the group in whole or in part, Mr. Jelesic's killings were found to be arbitrary. In that instance the Court abided by in dubio pro reo. In our instant case, there has not been any proof of any such nefarious activities by General Mladic. Furthermore, from the Perisic Appeals Chamber, it can be deduced that when the evidentiary base comprises one or more contradictory testimonies, or other forms of inconsistent evidence, it is not satisfactory that the Chamber merely acknowledges its existence. An analysis of such evidence together with a reckoning as to why it was or was not relied upon must be given as well. In light of all the arguments presented, the Defence submits that General Ratko Mladic is entitled to a dismissal of the charge relating to him entertaining genocidal intent for the reason that the Prosecution has not submitted sufficient evidence to support the charges. Your Honours, that concludes my presentation. On behalf of General Mladic and the rest of the Defence team, I thank you for listening to our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Groome, you were scheduled to start tomorrow. I think it would be wiser to wait until tomorrow so that you have an opportunity to better prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then before we adjourn, Mr. Ivetic, I asked for the source of the quote which was then given to me page 39 of the Assembly Session in Banja Luka. Perhaps -- you quoted as follows, referring to General Mladic specifically opposing the adoption of the six strategic goals at the Assembly. And then you quoted him as saying: "We have to call upon any man who has bowed his forehead to the ground to embrace these areas and the territory of the state we plan to make. He too has his place with us and next to us." What I found on page 39 is a quote, and I'm focusing on "forehead" because ... "We invite anyone whose forehead has touched this here, but first a Serb, I will not assign anyone else to a command duty. But I will assign someone no matter who he is." That is the quote I found on page 39 of the English translation. You then continued saying: "And he goes on further to say: 'But that does not mean Muslims have to be expelled or drowned.'" First of all, I had some difficulties in combining the first few lines with this then follow-up, which seems to be a bit inconsistent. And therefore I wondered -- first of all, I did not find anything on page 39 in the -- in close connection to the first quote, saying that it does not mean that Muslims have to be expelled or drowned. But I was wondering whether you were working from a different English translation and perhaps it would be wise, since you draw our attention to the fact what this fragment shows, that you would verify whether there was any issue about the English version of the Banja Luka Assembly Session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour. I was working off a snap-shot of a portion of the PDF of a translation. I don't know -- I'll have to check to see if that's the one that was in e-court. I thought it was and I will report back so that Mr. Groome knows before he begins tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- what the particular -- what exactly is the reference if it is something that is in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least it's a page where the word "forehead" appears, and from what I tried to search I find it nowhere in the transcript. But it seems that Mr. Mladic would like to consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. My client also remembers the words in -- says it's in relation to the SFRY. I will of course check the official exhibit as it is entered into the record and will report back informally to the Chamber and the other side via e-mail so they have time to prepare. And then I'm prepared tomorrow to on the record set forth what the results are of my inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because if there's any translation issue, we would rather know now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then at any later point in time. Nothing else at this moment. We adjourn for the day and we'll hear the Prosecution's submissions tomorrow, the 18th of March, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of March, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.
